avian seroprevalences are a reliable indicator of the risk of human WNV infection and that the risk of WNND cases is highest in years of low avian seroprevlance.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the antecedent immunity of avian maintenance hosts is an important determinant of the magnitude of subsequent outbreaks of WNV in the human population.
the maintenance of avian immunity in the face of WNV infection is a critical factor in limiting the amplification of this virus and the risk of human disease.

WNV transmission is a three-year cycle, with the first year being a period of silent introduction, the second year a period of rapid amplification and outbreak, and the third year a period of subsidence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
antecedent avian immunity limits the amplification of WNV and the subsequent tangential transmission of WNV to humans and horses.
antecedent avian immunity is the key determinant of WNV outbreaks.
WNV outbreaks in Los Angeles were driven by the antecedent serological status of avian hosts.
